questions.question: Two fish species live in the same lake. Why doesn't one eliminate the other?
questions.solution: Habitat is the ADDRESS (the lake); niche is the PROFESSION — what it eats, at what depth, at what time, at what temperature. The two species partition the lake's resources (surface feeder vs bottom feeder), so they compete less than they would if their niches overlapped fully. Resource partitioning allows coexistence.

questions.question: Classify these as abiotic or biotic and say how each limits a population: rainfall, a predator, soil pH, a competing species.
questions.solution: Abiotic: rainfall (water availability caps plant growth, hence food), soil pH (limits which nutrients are available). Biotic: a predator (removes individuals directly), a competitor (denies resources). Abiotic factors set the physical envelope; biotic factors act through other organisms — both shape where and how many can live.

questions.question: Give one morphological, one physiological and one behavioural adaptation of desert organisms.
questions.solution: Morphological: thick cuticle/spines and reduced leaf area (cut water loss) — e.g. cactus. Physiological: CAM metabolism — stomata open at night, storing CO₂ as organic acids for daytime photosynthesis. Behavioural: nocturnal activity and burrowing by day to avoid heat. Each level of biology contributes its own solution to the same problem.

questions.question: Classify with +/−/0: lichen, cattle egret and cattle, tapeworm and human.
questions.solution: Lichen: mutualism (+/+) — alga feeds, fungus shelters. Egret–cattle: commensalism (+/0) — egret feeds on insects flushed by cattle; cattle unaffected. Tapeworm–human: parasitism (+/−) — parasite benefits, host harmed. The sign pattern of who benefits and who loses defines the interaction.

questions.question: Why can a pyramid of energy never be inverted, while a pyramid of numbers sometimes can?
questions.solution: Energy shrinks ~90% at each transfer (heat loss, respiration) — a top predator's energy can never exceed its prey's total, so the energy pyramid is always upright. Numbers can invert: one tree supports thousands of insects (one producer, many consumers). Energy is one-way and dissipative; count is not.
